title: Ending Antidepressants II
subtitle: A conversation with Dr. Mark Horowitz, of Outro Health.
body_html:
Readers of The Frontier Psychiatrists, today’s article is part 2 of an interview with Dr. Mark Horowitz, MBBS, Ph.D. It has light editing. I’m your interviewer, Owen Scott Muir, M.D.

Part one is available here.

Part two is available here.

Part three is available here.

He’s a psychiatrist and co-founder of Outro Health. I’m an advisor to that company also. They exist to allow patients to taper off of antidepressant medication safely. I’ve written about the lack of efficacy in these drugs before.

My book, Inessential Pharmacology, does not go easy on drugs (Amazon link). Mark’s book is the Maudsley Deprescribing Guide. It offers guidance to clinicians on how to safely discontinue these medicines.

In part one, we learned that Mark trained as a psychiatrist and psychologist (at once!) in Australia and traveled to the UK to pursue neuroscience research. However, his brain problems were offered treatment with medicines that, themselves, caused side effects, and those piled up to a disabling condition…and the thing that almost killed him…was trying to stop. The story continues!

Subscribe now

MH: The bit that almost killed me was coming off the drugs initially.

OM: One of them is Xyrem, which can absolutely kill you. [ed: abrupt withdrawal from Xyrem (generic: Sodium Oxybate) can lead to seizures and death]

MH: It wasn't the Xyrem! It was coming off Lexapro (escitalopram).

OM: Wow.

MH: That was pretty close to not surviving.

OM: Oh, my gosh.

MH: Towards the end of my PhD, I came across a paper talking about withdrawal effects from antidepressants. I found that very startling because I hadn't encountered talk about withdrawal effects from antidepressants in either medical school or my training.

One, drugs that cause withdrawal effects also cause tolerance because they're the flip side of the same coin. So I thought, I've now been on a drug for 13 years at that point. How could it still be having any beneficial effect? Number one and number two drugs that cause withdrawal effects are generally not all that good for you.

You know, benzodiazepines, oxycontin. These are not drugs that you want to be on long-term. And so I found that jarring. It had been on my list. Maybe to try coming off my drug and reading that paper knocked it up to the top of my list. And so what I did was. I, you know, I'm a very nerdy human being.

I went and read all the academic literature about how to come off antidepressants. And a lot of it was written by people I was working with. I was working with professors at Oxford and Cambridge. They all said the same thing. Withdrawal effects from antidepressants are mild and last a week or two.

And you can avoid them by coming off over about four weeks. Well, that sounds reassuring. And then, because I'm a millennial—a geriatric millennial— I went and read online. I went to Google:

MH: I encountered a quite different narrative. People online said it was incredibly hard and took them months or years. Sometimes, I read that it could create much worse states. Even worse than the issues that people went on the drugs for. I’m an “institutionalized person.” I've got six degrees. I spend a lot of time listening to professors. I didn't know whose opinion to take! I decided to split the difference and to come off over four months, not four weeks, but not four years. I did that by getting a liquid version of the drug and using a micropipette from my biological psychiatry laboratory. So, I used the equipment I was familiar with from the lab.

OM: Is there an irony there?

MH: Yes. I was shuffling equipment out of the lab at night to measure small doses at home. I turned into a kind of Walter White character! I halved my dose every month for about four months. I was on 20 milligrams, I think, to start with or 15 milligrams, and by then, I was at one milligram.

I got down to one milligram, and my life basically imploded. I had trouble sleeping, and every morning, I would wake up in full-blown panic, even terror. But I had an experience in my life before. It was animal-level terror, like wild animals chasing me on the edge of a cliff.

I hadn't experienced before heart beating, palm sweaty, and that would last for about 10 hours of the day. By nighttime, I'd get a little bit of relief. I took up running, which would be a bit of relief. I ran so much my feet. I listened to hundreds, if not thousands, of repeats of body scan meditations.

It went on week after week after week. At some point in there, I thought, I'm not sure I can keep living like this. This is so unpleasant day after day. I was dizzy. Things around me appeared unreal. There wasn't a single second where I thought this was me returning. At 21, I was a miserable human being.

I was pessimistic. I was ruminatory. I'd never had a panic attack in my life….and here I was. I'd never had trouble sleeping. I'd never been thinking of ending my life. What I experienced at age 21? That was a 3/10 existential-level dilemma. What I lived through when I stopped the drugs? That was 9.75 out of 10. Eventually, I thought I couldn't keep going like this.

I went back on my drug. I returned to 20 milligrams, even higher than I've been on before.

OM: Oh, wow. That says a lot!

MH: I realized I was now on this drug, not because it was helpful, but because I couldn't stop it. I was now on this drug. I met every definition of being physically dependent on this drug.

What a cliffhanger for the end of part II!

Thanks for reading, and keep following my interview with Dr. Horowitz.
